claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Stag2 is required for mouse embryonic development.
claims.source: Thus, Stag2 is required for mouse embryonic development, consistent with a previous report (De Koninck et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Stag2null embryos die early, and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Stag1 and Stag2 have nonredundant developmental functions.
claims.source: Stag1 and Stag2 have nonredundant developmental functions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both Stag1 and Stag2 are individually required for development.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre pups presented growth retardation and premature death.
claims.source: The progenies were born in the Mendelian ratio, but Stag2f/y;NesCre pups presented growth retardation and premature death (Figure 1E, G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1E, G.

claims.claim: More than 50% Stag2f/y;NesCre mice died aged about 3 weeks while the rest died at about 4 months.
claims.source: More than 50% Stag2f/y;NesCre mice died aged about 3 weeks while the rest died at about 4 months.
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival curve data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y mice did not show differences discernible from wild-type (WT) littermates.
claims.source: Stag2f/y mice did not show differences discernible from wild-type (WT) littermates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice exhibited frequent hydrocephaly.
claims.source: Although Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not present microcephaly, they exhibited frequent hydrocephaly that might contribute to their premature death.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: Hydrocephaly might contribute to premature death in Stag2f/y;NesCre mice.
claims.source: Although Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not present microcephaly, they exhibited frequent hydrocephaly that might contribute to their premature death.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of hydrocephaly.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice displayed normal drinking and feeding behaviors.
claims.source: The Stag2f/y;NesCre mice displayed normal drinking and feeding behaviors (Figure 1H), but showed reduced plasma IGF-1 levels compared to the control mice (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by metabolic cage analysis data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed reduced plasma IGF-1 levels compared to control mice.
claims.source: The Stag2f/y;NesCre mice displayed normal drinking and feeding behaviors (Figure 1H), but showed reduced plasma IGF-1 levels compared to the control mice (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IGF-1 measurement data shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping.
claims.source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping (Figure 1K) and limb tremors (Video 1), which were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1K.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed limb tremors.
claims.source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping (Figure 1K) and limb tremors (Video 1), which were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Video 1.

claims.claim: Forepaw and hindlimb clasping and limb tremors were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
claims.source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping (Figure 1K) and limb tremors (Video 1), which were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: Stag2 deficiency in the nervous system causes growth retardation and neurological defects.
claims.source: These data indicate that Stag2 deficiency in the nervous system causes growth retardation and neurological defects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic observations of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice.

claims.claim: H&E staining of brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not reveal overt anatomical defects.
claims.source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not reveal overt anatomical defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The differentiation of neurons and astrocytes in Stag2-deleted brains was largely normal.
claims.source: As revealed by immunohistochemistry assays using neuron- or astrocyte-specific antibodies, the differentiation of neurons and astrocytes in Stag2-deleted brains was largely normal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E.

claims.claim: 105 genes were significantly downregulated by more than twofolds in Stag2-deficient brains at post-natal day 21.
claims.source: Compared with the control groups, 105 and 62 genes were significantly down- or upregulated by more than twofolds, respectively, in the Stag2-deficient brains.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claims.claim: 62 genes were significantly upregulated by more than twofolds in Stag2-deficient brains at post-natal day 21.
claims.source: Compared with the control groups, 105 and 62 genes were significantly down- or upregulated by more than twofolds, respectively, in the Stag2-deficient brains.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claims.claim: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs in the brains of Stag2 cKO mice, 44 were enriched in myelin.
claims.source: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs in the brains of Stag2 cKO mice, 44 were enriched in myelin (Figure 2C; Thakurela et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis and comparison with myelin-enriched gene lists from previous literature.

claims.claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis pathways are the most affected canonical pathways in Stag2 cKO brains.
claims.source: The ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) pinpoints cholesterol biosynthesis pathways as the most affected canonical pathways (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IPA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis precursors were reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
claims.source: We further confirmed that the cholesterol biosynthesis precursors were reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Myelin is the membrane sheath that wraps around axons to facilitate rapid nerve conduction and maintain metabolic supply.
claims.source: Myelin is the membrane sheath that wraps around axons to facilitate rapid nerve conduction and maintain metabolic supply (Williamson and Lyons, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Dynamic myelination in the central nervous system (CNS) is critical for proper neurodevelopment.
claims.source: Dynamic myelination in the central nervous system (CNS) is critical for proper neurodevelopment, and defective myelination is associated with autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases (Mathys et al., 2019; Wolf et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Defective myelination is associated with autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases.
claims.source: Dynamic myelination in the central nervous system (CNS) is critical for proper neurodevelopment, and defective myelination is associated with autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases (Mathys et al., 2019; Wolf et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis is essential for normal myelination.
claims.source: Cholesterol biosynthesis is essential for normal myelination (Hubler et al., 2018; Saher et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed greatly reduced luxol fast blue (LFB) staining compared to those of Stag2f/y and NesCre heterozygous mice at about P21.
claims.source: Indeed, brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed greatly reduced luxol fast blue (LFB) staining compared to those of Stag2f/y and NesCre heterozygous mice at about P21 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LFB staining data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Stag2 cKO mice had significant defects in myelin fiber formation at P18-P21.
claims.source: Immunohistochemistry using antibodies against myelin proteins, Myelin basic protein (MBP) and Proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1), confirmed that Stag2 cKO mice had significant defects in myelin fiber formation at P18-P21 (Figure 3B–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B–F.

claims.claim: In both cerebral cortex and cerebellum, there were fewer and sparser myelin fibers in Stag2f/y;NesCre mice, as compared to the Stag2f/y controls.
claims.source: In both cerebral cortex and cerebellum, there were fewer and sparser myelin fibers in Stag2f/y;NesCre mice, as compared to the Stag2f/y controls.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and quantification data.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice at P18 had significantly fewer myelin-wrapped axons at optic nerves.
claims.source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice at P18 had significantly fewer myelin-wrapped axons at optic nerves.
claims.evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Myelination predominantly occurs at 3 weeks after birth in the mouse.
claims.source: Myelination predominantly occurs at 3 weeks after birth in the mouse.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claims.claim: The timing of premature death of Stag2 cKO mice is consistent with defective myelination as a contributing factor to the lethality.
claims.source: The timing of premature death of Stag2 cKO mice is thus consistent with defective myelination as a contributing factor to the lethality.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between the timing of myelination and the timing of death.

claims.claim: Both Stag1 and Stag2 were expressed at high levels in hippocampus, medial habenula, neocortex, and cerebellum granular layer.
claims.source: Both Stag1 and Stag2 were expressed at high levels in hippocampus, medial habenula, neocortex, and cerebellum granular layer.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Stag2 transcripts were detected at relatively high levels in subventricular zone, thalamus, fiber tracts, midbrain, and hindbrain regions.
claims.source: Aside from these regions, the Stag2 transcripts were detected at relatively high levels in subventricular zone, thalamus, fiber tracts, midbrain, and hindbrain regions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Stag2 is ubiquitously expressed in the brain.
claims.source: Stag2 is thus ubiquitously expressed in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the in situ hybridization data showing widespread expression.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are responsible for myelination in the CNS.
claims.source: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are responsible for myelination in the CNS.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claims.claim: The two genotype groups (Stag2f/y;NesCre and Stag2f/y) had similar cellular compositions in scRNA-seq analysis.
claims.source: As revealed by clusters in the t-SNE plot, the two genotype groups had similar cellular compositions (Figure 4A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claims.claim: All cell clusters were present in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
claims.source: All cell clusters were present in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains, again indicating generally normal neural cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Stag2 ablation occurred early in the NPC stage and was maintained in all differentiated cell lineages.
claims.source: Based on the expression changes of Stag2 and other cohesin genes in OLs, astrocytes, and neuronal lineages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), it is clear that Stag2 ablation occurred early in the NPC stage and was maintained in all differentiated cell lineages.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on scRNA-seq data showing Stag2 expression changes across cell types.

claims.claim: There was a mild reduction in the proportion of MOLs in Stag2f/y;NesCre forebrains.
claims.source: Quantification of the distributions of these five cell types within the OL lineage revealed a mild reduction in the proportion of MOLs in Stag2f/y forebrains (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: More cells were present in the terminal maturation stages in the Stag2f/y brains.
claims.source: The reclustering of single cells in the OL lineage along the pseudotime path revealed that more cells were present in the terminal maturation stages in the Stag2f/y brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, F.

claims.claim: More cells were retained at the undifferentiated stages in the Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
claims.source: Conversely, more cells were retained at the undifferentiated stages in the Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
claims.evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis data.

claims.claim: Some myelination genes, including Myelin and lymphocyte protein (Mal), were specifically repressed in Stag2f/y;NesCre MOLs.
claims.source: Strikingly, some myelination genes, including Myelin and lymphocyte protein (Mal), were specifically repressed in Stag2f/y;NesCre MOLs, with their expression in nonneural cells unaltered (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: STAG2 deficiency delays the maturation of OLs.
claims.source: These observations suggest that STAG2 deficiency delays the maturation of OLs and compromises myelination-specific gene expression in mature OLs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on trajectory analysis and gene expression data.

claims.claim: STAG2 deficiency compromises myelination-specific gene expression in mature OLs.
claims.source: These observations suggest that STAG2 deficiency delays the maturation of OLs and compromises myelination-specific gene expression in mature OLs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on scRNA-seq data showing reduced expression of myelination genes.

claims.claim: Stag1 transcripts are less abundant in the OL lineage compared to Stag2 and genes encoding other cohesin core subunits, except for cycling OPCs.
claims.source: Interestingly, compared to Stag2 and genes encoding other cohesin core subunits, Stag1 transcripts are less abundant in the OL lineage, except for cycling OPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C.

claims.claim: The low expression of Stag1 in mature OLs might make these cells more dependent on Stag2 for function.
claims.source: The low expression of Stag1 in mature OLs might make these cells more dependent on Stag2 for function.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of low Stag1 expression in mature OLs.

claims.claim: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 271 genes were downregulated by more than two folds.
claims.source: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 271 and 292 genes were downregulated or upregulated by more than two folds, respectively (Figure 4F and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data of isolated primary OLs shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 292 genes were upregulated by more than two folds.
claims.source: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 271 and 292 genes were downregulated or upregulated by more than two folds, respectively (Figure 4F and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data of isolated primary OLs shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The downregulated genes in Stag2-deleted OLs were generally highly expressed in WT cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the downregulated genes were generally highly expressed in WT cells, whereas the upregulated genes had low expression levels in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D.

claims.claim: The upregulated genes in Stag2-deleted OLs had low expression levels in WT cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the downregulated genes were generally highly expressed in WT cells, whereas the upregulated genes had low expression levels in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D.

claims.claim: The top pathways enriched in the downregulated DEGs in Stag2-deleted OLs included the cholesterol and small molecule biosynthetic pathways and oligodendrocyte differentiation.
claims.source: The top pathways enriched in the downregulated DEGs included the cholesterol and small molecule biosynthetic pathways and oligodendrocyte differentiation (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Cilium organization and assembly are the top enriched pathways in the upregulated DEGs in Stag2-deleted OLs.
claims.source: Cilium organization and assembly are the top enriched pathways in the upregulated DEGs (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs identified by RNA-seq analysis of the whole brain of Stag2-deficient mice, 42 were also differentially expressed in primary oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs identified by RNA-seq analysis of the whole brain of Stag2-deficient mice, 42 were also differentially expressed in primary oligodendrocytes (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from whole brain and isolated OLs shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Defective cholesterol biosynthesis and oligodendrocyte differentiation likely underly hypomyelination and neurological defects in Stag2 cKO mice.
claims.source: Thus, defective cholesterol biosynthesis and oligodendrocyte differentiation likely underly hypomyelination and neurological defects in Stag2 cKO mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the pathway analysis and gene expression data.

claims.claim: Stag2 loss did not appreciably affect H3K27Ac enrichment at transcription start sites (TSSs).
claims.source: We performed chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) experiments to examine the enrichment of the active transcription mark H3K27ac in Stag2f/y and Stag2f/y;NesCre OLs and found that Stag2 loss did not appreciably affect H3K27Ac enrichment at transcription start sites (TSSs) (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claims.claim: The upregulated genes had much lower H3K27ac enrichment near their TSS, indicating that they were less active.
claims.source: Consistent with our RNA-seq results, the upregulated genes had much lower H3K27ac enrichment near their TSS, indicating that they were less active.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq data showing lower H3K27ac enrichment at upregulated genes.

claims.claim: STAG2 was enriched at TSS of stable and downregulated genes, including genes in the cholesterol biosynthesis and myelination pathways.
claims.source: Among other genomic loci, STAG2 was enriched at TSS of stable and downregulated genes, including genes in the cholesterol biosynthesis and myelination pathways (Figure 5C, D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by STAG2 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C, D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Among the 271 downregulated DEGs, there were 210 genes (77%) with STAG2 enrichment near the transcriptional start site (TSS ± 2 kb).
claims.source: Among the 271 downregulated DEGs, there were 210 genes (77%) with STAG2 enrichment near the transcriptional start site (TSS ± 2 kb).
claims.evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: STAG2 occupied the promoter regions of many downregulated DEGs in oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Thus, STAG2 occupied the promoter regions of many downregulated DEGs in oligodendrocytes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq data showing STAG2 enrichment at promoters of downregulated genes.

claims.claim: STAG2 was enriched at the TSS of upregulated genes to a lesser extent, with only 117 of the 292 (40%) upregulated DEGs exhibiting STAG2 ChIP-seq peaks at their TSS ± 2 kb regions.
claims.source: It was enriched at the TSS of upregulated genes to a lesser extent, with only 117 of the 292 (40%) upregulated DEGs exhibiting STAG2 ChIP-seq peaks at their TSS ± 2 kb regions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Stag2 loss might have indirectly affected the expression of less active genes.
claims.source: Stag2 loss might have indirectly affected the expression of these less active genes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that upregulated genes have lower STAG2 binding.

claims.claim: Few compartment switching events were observed in Stag2-deleted cells.
claims.source: We observed few compartment switching events in Stag2-deleted cells (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claims.claim: Virtually all genomic regions in Stag2-deleted cells were kept in their original compartment categories (AA or BB).
claims.source: Virtually all genomic regions in Stag2-deleted cells were kept in their original compartment categories (AA or BB) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: More genes located in the transcriptionally active A compartment (AA) were repressed in Stag2-deleted cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data, analysis of average gene expression changes of DEGs in these genomic regions revealed that more genes located in the transcriptionally active A compartment (AA) were repressed in Stag2-deleted cells and more genes in the transcriptionally silent B compartment (BB) were upregulated (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by integration of Hi-C and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: More genes in the transcriptionally silent B compartment (BB) were upregulated in Stag2-deleted cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data, analysis of average gene expression changes of DEGs in these genomic regions revealed that more genes located in the transcriptionally active A compartment (AA) were repressed in Stag2-deleted cells and more genes in the transcriptionally silent B compartment (BB) were upregulated (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by integration of Hi-C and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Genes that switched from the A compartment to the B compartment were not more repressed compared to those that remained in the A compartment.
claims.source: Genes that switched from the A compartment to the B compartment were not more repressed compared to those that remained in the A compartment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression changes in different compartment categories.

claims.claim: Genes located in chromatin regions that switched from compartment B to A were not significantly activated compared to genes that stayed in the B compartment.
claims.source: Likewise, compared to genes that stayed in the B compartment, genes located in chromatin regions that switched from compartment B to A were not significantly activated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression changes in different compartment categories.

claims.claim: Acute depletion of all forms of cohesin eliminates TAD formation.
claims.source: Acute depletion of all forms of cohesin eliminates TAD formation (Wutz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Deletion of Stag2 had minimal impact on TAD formation in oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: In contrast, deletion of Stag2 had minimal impact on TAD formation in oligodendrocytes (Figure 6E–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that STAG1-cohesin compensates for the loss of STAG2-cohesin in spatial organization of chromatin at larger than megabase scales.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis data shown in Figure 6E–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: STAG1-cohesin compensates for the loss of STAG2-cohesin in spatial organization of chromatin at larger than megabase scales.
claims.source: In contrast, deletion of Stag2 had minimal impact on TAD formation in oligodendrocytes (Figure 6E–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that STAG1-cohesin compensates for the loss of STAG2-cohesin in spatial organization of chromatin at larger than megabase scales.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TADs are maintained despite Stag2 loss.

claims.claim: Compartment switching and TAD alterations are not the underlying cause for the observed gene expression changes in STAG2-deficient OLs.
claims.source: Therefore, our analyses did not uncover evidence for compartment switching and TAD alterations being the underlying cause for the observed gene expression changes in STAG2-deficient OLs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Hi-C analysis showing minimal compartment and TAD changes.

claims.claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre OLs had significantly fewer loops across almost all genomic distances compared to Stag2f/y OLs.
claims.source: Compared to Stag2f/y OLs, Stag2f/y;NesCre OLs had significantly fewer loops across almost all genomic distances (Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data shown in Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Loops specific to Stag2f/y;NesCre OLs were longer than STAG2-dependent Stag2f/y-specific loops.
claims.source: Loops specific to Stag2f/y;NesCre OLs, which were likely mediated by STAG1-cohesin, were longer than STAG2-dependent Stag2f/y-specific loops.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data.

claims.claim: When genomic distances exceeded 0.25 Mb, the loops from Stag2f/y;NesCre cells gradually gained higher scores over loops from Stag2f/y cells.
claims.source: When genomic distances exceeded 0.25 Mb, the loops from Stag2f/y;NesCre cells gradually gained higher scores over loops from Stag2f/y cells (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: STAG1-cohesin cannot completely compensate for STAG2-cohesin during loop formation.
claims.source: Therefore, STAG1-cohesin cannot completely compensate for STAG2-cohesin during loop formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Stag2-deleted cells have fewer loops.

claims.claim: STAG1-cohesin-mediated loops are relatively longer than STAG2-cohesin-mediated loops.
claims.source: STAG1-cohesin-mediated loops are relatively longer than STAG2-cohesin-mediated loops, consistent with published findings in HeLa cells (Wutz et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data and a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Loops anchored at gene promoters, including those of downregulated genes, were reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: When examining the local Hi-C maps, we noticed that loops anchored at gene promoters, including those of downregulated genes, were reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre oligodendrocytes (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C, and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: The total number of P-loops was proportionally decreased in Stag2f/y;NesCre cells.
claims.source: The total number of P-loops was proportionally decreased in Stag2f/y;NesCre cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: The loops anchored at the downregulated genes were stronger than those at upregulated and stable genes.
claims.source: Moreover, the loops anchored at the downregulated genes were stronger than those at upregulated and stable genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Loop enrichment at promoters of downregulated genes was reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre cells to a greater extent than that at promoters of upregulated and stable genes.
claims.source: Loop enrichment at promoters of downregulated genes was reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre cells to a greater extent than that at promoters of upregulated and stable genes (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pile-up analysis of Hi-C data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Among the 162 downregulated DEGs with reduced promoter-anchored loops in the Stag2-depleted cells, 137 genes (85%) had STAG2 peaks in their promoter regions (TSS ± 2 kb).
claims.source: Among the 162 downregulated DEGs with reduced promoter-anchored loops in the Stag2-depleted cells, 137 genes (85%) had STAG2 peaks in their promoter regions (TSS ± 2 kb).
claims.evidence: This is supported by integration of Hi-C and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The loops anchored at downregulated genes with STAG2 binding had significantly higher loop scores, compared to those with no STAG2 binding.
claims.source: The loops anchored at downregulated genes with STAG2 binding had significantly higher loop scores, compared to those with no STAG2 binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C, D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C, D.

claims.claim: The stronger looping at promoters of downregulated genes with STAG2 binding might be maintained by STAG1-cohesin or other factors in Stag2-deleted cells.
claims.source: This difference was still observed in Stag2-deleted cells, suggesting that the stronger looping at these gene promoters might be maintained by STAG1-cohesin or other factors in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that loop scores remain higher at these genes even after Stag2 deletion.

claims.claim: The loops anchored at upregulated genes with STAG2 binding had lower loop scores.
claims.source: By contrast, the loops anchored at upregulated genes with STAG2 binding had lower loop scores.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data.

claims.claim: The loop scores of loops anchored at stable genes were not affected by STAG2 occupancy.
claims.source: The loop scores of loops anchored at stable genes were not affected by STAG2 occupancy.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C loop analysis data.

claims.claim: Stag2 loss diminishes the number of, but not the strength, short chromosome loops, including promoter-anchored loops.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest that Stag2 loss diminishes the number of, but not the strength, short chromosome loops, including promoter-anchored loops.

results.result: The authors generated a Stag2 floxed mouse line by targeting exon 8 on the X chromosome. Complete knockout (Stag2null) embryos showed severe developmental defects and necrosis by E11.5, demonstrating that Stag2 is required for embryonic development. Combined with the requirement for Stag1, this establishes that Stag1 and Stag2 have nonredundant developmental functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 provide direct experimental evidence from mouse genetics showing Stag2null embryos die early (C32), supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B. The conclusion that Stag2 is required for development (C33) is well-supported and consistent with cited literature (C33). The inference of nonredundancy (C34) logically follows from both Stag1 and Stag2 being individually essential.

results.result: Nervous system-specific deletion of Stag2 (Stag2f/y;NesCre mice) causes growth retardation, premature death (>50% by 3 weeks, remainder by 4 months), neurological defects including limb clasping and tremors, hydrocephaly, and reduced plasma IGF-1 levels, while feeding and drinking behaviors remain normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C44 are supported by multiple experimental observations including survival curves (Figure 1G), body weight measurements (Figure 1F), behavioral assessments (Figure 1K, Video 1), and IGF-1 measurements (Figure 1J). The phenotypic characterization is comprehensive with appropriate controls (Stag2f/y mice). The inference that Stag2 deficiency causes these phenotypes (C45) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of Stag2 cKO brains at P21 revealed 105 downregulated and 62 upregulated genes (>2-fold change), with 44 of the downregulated genes enriched in myelin. Cholesterol biosynthesis pathways were the most affected canonical pathways, confirmed by reduced cholesterol biosynthesis precursors in Stag2 cKO brains.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2A-D), RT-qPCR validation (Figure 2B), pathway analysis (Figure 2D), and mass spectrometry confirmation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F). The analysis includes appropriate biological replicates (n=4 pairs) and statistical validation. The histological observations (C46-C47) provide important context showing no gross anatomical defects.

results.result: Stag2 cKO mice exhibit hypomyelination as evidenced by reduced luxol fast blue staining, decreased MBP and PLP1 immunostaining in cortex and cerebellum, and fewer myelin-wrapped axons in optic nerves at P18-P21. The timing of premature death correlates with the period of active myelination (3 weeks postnatal).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by multiple complementary techniques: LFB staining (Figure 3A), immunohistochemistry with quantification (Figure 3B-F), and transmission electron microscopy (Figure 3G). The data include appropriate statistical analysis and biological replicates. The temporal correlation between myelination timing and lethality (C62) is a reasonable inference, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of P13 forebrains revealed similar cellular compositions between genotypes with all cell clusters present. However, trajectory analysis showed delayed oligodendrocyte maturation in Stag2 cKO brains, with more cells retained at undifferentiated stages and specific repression of myelination genes (e.g., Mal) in mature oligodendrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C73 are supported by scRNA-seq data with appropriate biological replicates (n=2 per genotype). The trajectory analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and cell-type-specific gene expression analysis (Figure 4D) provide strong evidence for delayed maturation. The inferences about STAG2 deficiency effects (C74-C75) are well-supported by the quantitative data, though the mechanistic basis remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Bulk RNA-seq of isolated primary oligodendrocytes revealed 271 downregulated and 292 upregulated genes (>2-fold) in Stag2-deleted cells. Downregulated genes were highly expressed in WT cells and enriched for cholesterol biosynthesis and oligodendrocyte differentiation pathways, while upregulated genes had low baseline expression and were enriched for cilium organization pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 are supported by bulk RNA-seq data from isolated primary OLs (Figure 4F-H) with appropriate pathway analysis (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5-6). The observation that downregulated genes are highly expressed while upregulated genes have low expression (C80-C81) is an important finding supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4B-D. The inference about defective cholesterol biosynthesis and oligodendrocyte differentiation (C85) is well-justified.

results.result: ChIP-seq analysis showed that Stag2 loss did not affect H3K27ac enrichment at TSSs globally. STAG2 was enriched at TSSs of stable and downregulated genes (77% of 271 downregulated genes had STAG2 peaks within TSS±2kb), including cholesterol biosynthesis and myelination genes, but was less enriched at upregulated genes (40%).
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 are supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 5A-D) showing STAG2 binding patterns and H3K27ac enrichment. The quantitative analysis of STAG2 occupancy at different gene categories is rigorous. The speculation that upregulated genes are indirectly affected (C92) is reasonable given the lower STAG2 binding, though alternative explanations exist.

results.result: Hi-C analysis revealed minimal compartment switching and preserved TAD structure in Stag2-deleted oligodendrocytes. While genes in the A compartment were preferentially downregulated and genes in the B compartment were upregulated, compartment switching itself did not correlate with gene expression changes. STAG1-cohesin appears to compensate for STAG2-cohesin loss at megabase scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C102 are supported by comprehensive Hi-C analysis (Figure 6) with biological replicates. The observation of minimal compartment switching (C93-C94) and preserved TADs (C100) is well-documented. The lack of correlation between compartment switching and gene expression changes (C97-C98) is an important negative result. The inference about STAG1 compensation (C101) is reasonable but remains speculative without direct STAG1 depletion experiments.

results.result: Stag2 deletion reduced the number of chromosome loops across most genomic distances, with STAG2-dependent loops being shorter than STAG1-mediated loops. Promoter-anchored loops at downregulated genes were preferentially reduced, with 85% of 162 downregulated genes with reduced P-loops having STAG2 peaks at their promoters. Loop strength was not reduced, only loop number.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C113 and C117 are supported by detailed Hi-C loop analysis (Figure 7) with reproducible results across replicates. The quantitative analysis of loop numbers, lengths, and strengths is rigorous. The integration with ChIP-seq data (C112) strengthens the conclusions. The distinction between loop number and strength (C117) is an important mechanistic insight supported by pile-up analysis (Figure 7E).

results.result: Pile-up analysis of Hi-C maps revealed asymmetric promoter-anchored stripes extending in the direction of transcription at downregulated genes, consistent with one-sided loop extrusion from promoter to gene body. These stripes persisted in Stag2-deleted cells, suggesting STAG1-cohesin can mediate their formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 and C146-C148 are supported by Hi-C pile-up analysis (Figure 7F). The observation of directional stripes (C119) is clear in the data. The interpretation as one-sided loop extrusion (C120, C147) is a reasonable inference based on the pattern, though direct evidence for the mechanism is lacking. The persistence of stripes in Stag2-deleted cells (C121, C148) supports STAG1 compensation, though this remains inferential.

results.result: The authors conclude that STAG2-cohesin generates promoter-anchored loops at myelination-promoting genes to facilitate their transcription, based on the correlation between reduced promoter-anchored loops and reduced gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C10 and C145 represent the central mechanistic conclusion integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq data. The correlation between reduced P-loops and gene downregulation is well-documented (C9, C108-C111). However, the causal relationship is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The conclusion is reasonable given the data, but alternative mechanisms (e.g., effects on transcription elongation, R-loop resolution) cannot be excluded.

results.result: The study implicates defective myelination as a contributing factor to cohesinopathy and establishes oligodendrocytes as a relevant cell type for studying cohesin-mediated transcription regulation. The authors suggest that hypomyelination is a major underlying cause for the Stag2 cKO phenotypes and that myelination defects may occur in human cohesinopathy patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C123 represent important translational conclusions. While the mouse data strongly support a role for myelination defects in the Stag2 cKO phenotype (C129-C130), the extrapolation to human cohesinopathy (C137-C138) is more speculative. The cited reports of myelination defects in CdLS patients (C138) provide some support, but STAG2 mutations are rare and hypomorphic in human disease (C134). The therapeutic speculation (C140) is premature without additional validation.

results.result: Stag1 transcripts are less abundant than Stag2 in the oligodendrocyte lineage (except cycling OPCs), which may make mature oligodendrocytes more dependent on Stag2 for function and explain why oligodendrocytes are more severely affected by Stag2 loss.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B-C) showing differential expression patterns. However, the speculation about functional dependence (C77, C151) is not directly tested. While the correlation between low Stag1 expression and oligodendrocyte sensitivity is suggestive, alternative explanations (discussed in C152-C157) are equally plausible and not distinguished by the data.

results.result: The authors propose three non-mutually exclusive models for how STAG2-mediated chromosome looping facilitates transcription: (1) promoter-enhancer loops bring enhancer factors to the promoter; (2) loop extrusion promotes transcription elongation by regulating R-loop formation and pre-mRNA processing; (3) promoter-terminator loops recycle RNA polymerase II.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C163 represent mechanistic models proposed in the Discussion. While these models are plausible and consistent with the data, they are largely speculative. The R-loop interaction data (C160-C161) from cited literature provides some support for model 2, but direct evidence for any of these mechanisms in oligodendrocytes is lacking. These represent hypotheses for future testing rather than supported conclusions.

results.result: In situ hybridization analysis showed that both Stag1 and Stag2 are expressed at high levels in hippocampus, medial habenula, neocortex, and cerebellum granular layer, with Stag2 also detected in subventricular zone, thalamus, fiber tracts, midbrain, and hindbrain, indicating ubiquitous brain expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The expression patterns are clearly documented, and the conclusion of ubiquitous expression (C65) is reasonable. This provides important context for understanding the cell-type-specific effects of Stag2 deletion.

results.result: The Introduction provides established background on cohesin function, composition, and disease relevance, including its role in chromosome folding, loop extrusion, TAD formation, transcription regulation, and mutations causing cohesinopathy and cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C29 represent background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These establish the scientific context for the study and are generally well-accepted in the field. The claims about Stag1 and Stag2 nonredundancy (C28-C29) are supported by cited literature and the authors' own data.
